#3972. PlayStation sees record high player numbers and increased revenue for Q2 2026, and a lot of that success is down to Marvel's Wolverine

As part of today's (Thursday 5th November, 2026) financial results, Sony has confirmed that monthly active users, referred to as MAU, across both PlayStation 4 and 5, reached 127 million in September. This represents a seven percent growth year-on-year for the company, and sets a new record high.

In Layman's terms, this simply means that more people are engaged with the PlayStation ecosystem now than ever before. And it's not just that there are more people using machines and occasionally booting up their consoles; active play time also increased over the past quarter, too, with total logged play time increasing by four percent, year-on-year. As a result, Sony and PlayStation noted that its Game & Network Services division saw revenue grow by nine percent year-on-year, resulting in operating profit rising by 83 percent year-on-year.

Notably, despite its mixed reception, Marvel's Wolverine was name-checked as a driving force for the decent performance over the past quarter - but that shouldn't be a surprise for anyone that's actually been paying attention to how the game performed. The game sold through 2.4 million copies as of 4th November (so, in roughly 50 days). Ghost of Yotei, meanwhile, has sold through 3.3 million since its launch in October 2025.

More people playing consoles, and for longer - it must all be good news for Sony right? Well, not all the graphs are showing growth. PS5 hardware sales continue to gradually decline: in the reporting period, Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 consoles, down from 4 million in the same quarter in 2025. But, with 100 million PS5 units out in the wild, and 127 million PlayStation accounts across the whole ecosystem, Sony doesn't seem that worried: instead, the company is now focusing on converting those with active accounts into more viable customers.

Elsewhere in the results, we heard from Sony CFO Lin Tao that the PlayStation 6 is on track and "progressing as scheduled", with "solid progress" expected on the machine in 2027. Regarding those falling PS5 sales, Tao also referenced that, and says it's all part of the natural cycle of console launches and iteration. "Although new PS5 unit sales are gradually declining as expected at this stage of the console life cycle, the PlayStation platform continues to expand and grow in a stable manner," Tao explained. "[Next year,] we intend to make solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform."

It must be encouraging for Sony to see this growth in this quarter, especially after all the bad press and furore around the company's decision to end the manufacturing of PlayStation discs by January 2028. It seems to be a core part of the gaming audience's understanding of game ownership, the decision has been widely contested as anti-consumer. It's caused a lot of bad blood with PlayStation players over the past six months, but - seemingly, given these results - that has translated to very little material impact on Sony's bottom line.

Despite its mixed reception, Marvel's Wolverine was September's top-selling new game in the US, making Sony launch revenues it hasn't seen since Helldivers 2

#3971. Nintendo game sales surge thanks to Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream, but Switch 2 hardware suffers big decline

Nintendo's latest financial earnings report is here, revealing healthy software sales thanks to the enormously popular Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. Sales of Switch 2 hardware, however, are down.

As per Nintendo's 2nd Quarter fiscal earnings report, focusing on the three-month period ending 30th September 2026, Switch 2 hardware registered a big drop in sales during the first half of the current financial year (FY27).

Over that period, Nintendo sold 6.49m Switch 2 units and 1.27m units of the original Switch - equating to a 37.4 percent decline for Switch 2 and 32.7 percent decline for Switch 1 compared to the same period last year. Nintendo had previously forecast a decline in hardware sales, and the company still expects to sell 16.50m Switch 2 units by the end of the current fiscal year.

Nintendo software sales, on the other hand, saw a big year-on-year boost of 18.8 percent on Switch 2 (to 24.49m units) and a smaller increase of 6.8 percent on Switch 1. That's all thanks to the release of several popular first- and third-party titles over the first half of FY27. Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream was by far the most successful game with 8.81m units sold, followed by Rhythm Heaven Groove at 2.89m. Splatoon Raiders (the only Switch 2 exclusive of the three) sold 2.42m. Nintendo also highlighted a 60.5 percent year-on-year increase in digital game sales.

The increase in software unit sales and the "continued weakness of the Yen" couldn't prevent the overall business from declining by 15.3 percent year-on-year, however.

Other remaining releases in Nintendo' s current fiscal year include The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (which launches today and was awarded five stars in Eurogamer's review), Switch 2 re-releases of Pikmin 2 and Xenoblade Chronicles 3, as well as Metroid Ravenous, which arrives early in 2027.

"Physical" copies of GTA 6 started shipping out to early buyers this week, including several members of GamesRadar+ staff. As players start to worry that their codes may be stolen with a bizarre flashlight trick, we had to see if we could steal our own – and honestly, I wouldn't be too worried about the possibility.

Rockstar's approach to its code-in-box release of GTA 6 is slightly different from most publishers. Rather than including the game code printed on a slip of paper in the case, the code is printed inside the back cover art itself. Social media is starting to be washed over with reports that if you shine a very bright flashlight just right into the edge of a GTA 6 case, you can make out the code without even breaking the seal on the game.

I tried the trick with my own US copy of the PS5 physical edition, and it did not work. There's a strip of camouflage patterning underneath the code that renders it unreadable from the opposite side no matter how bright a light you shine at it. My colleague Catherine tried the trick with her UK PS5 copy, and same deal – the code is unreadable through that camo pattern.

There is a catch here: not every code-in-box copy of GTA 6 has the camo strip. I've combed through unboxing videos of the game, and while I can't find any examples of US copies without the protective camouflage, some copies with a PEGI rating only have a plain black strip in the background. This, it seems, is the one that could be vulnerable to the apparent flashlight trick.

However, I haven't managed to track down anybody reporting that they've fallen victim to a stolen code. Most retailers keep their games behind locked glass cases, so a prospective code thief would probably have to buy the game, hope that it's a black background version, get an unusually powerful flashlight, shine it in, and then convince the retailer to take the game back for a refund in order for anyone to fall afoul of the potential scam.

Is that a level of trouble anyone's willing to go to in order to play GTA 6 for free? Well, yeah, I guess so. But it's also not an issue unique to GTA's code-in-box release – I've had a few occasions where I've purchased a new, "sealed" copy of a traditional physical game only to find that someone had carefully snuck the disc out of the package and returned it to the retailer where I eventually bought it.

And, well, if you're that worried, you can just buy the game digitally. Yeah, I know, I'm the exact kind of sicko who bought the physical version to have a box on my shelf and a poster on my wall, but it's not as if there's a real difference between getting the box and just doing a digital GTA 6 pre-order. Now, if there was actually a map in the box, that might be a different story.

#3969. Echoes of Mirror's Edge, Dishonored and a dream set in Italy I once had can be found in Boars in Rome, an expressive parkour platformer set in dystopian Rome

Years ago, I had this dream where I was parkouring through a greatly sunken version of Venice, no doubt sourced from the many hours I put into Assassin's Creed 2 as a teen who should have been studying for their GCSEs a lot more than they were. It's stuck with me after all this time mostly because of how much I wanted to capture that feeling again somehow, as the real Assassin's Creed didn't quite cut it. And lo and behold, there I was today browsing Bluesky when I came across Boars in Rome, a Mirror's Edge and Counter Strike Surf inspired parkour platformer set in a dystopian version of Rome.

Truthfully, witnessing the clip I've shared below was baffling to me. "This is what I dreamt of!" More or less, anyway, for the setting isn't quite the same; "You have been selected to start a new life off planet. Earth has been abandoned," explains the game's Steam page. "Machines keep working and nature claims what remains. Find out what happened while you were frozen in time by exploring the remnants of Rome where historical monuments mix with futurist megastructures."

Mirrors Edge x Counter Strike Surf where you parkour on anything! Be smooth n stylish in dystopian Rome. Or just jump around and explore, whatever works for you. It's called Boars in Rome! #PitchYaGame[image or embed]

Not all of it matches that dream of mine, some of it leans much more into brutalism than the typical, much older architecture you'd expect of Rome, but it's there nonetheless. In motion, Boars in Rome feels quite oneiric too. There is so much more control over the game's avatar than what my real body is capable of, or wants to do. You can run, jump, slide and wallrun, positioning it quite closely to VHOLUME mechanically. Where it differs is in its additives, movement tech like being able to swing on lampposts or vault over low down obstacles.

VHOLUME is more of a game about providing you with a simple toolkit and leaving you to push it to its maximum. Boars in Roam is a touch more expressive, and I'd dare to even call it an immersive sim. The levels you can romp around are linear, you have an end point to reach, only the journey is up to you. It certainly feels appropriate to put it in the im sim camp given that, at least the game's first level, calls to mind Viktor Antonov's work on Dishonored (and Half-Life 2, too, honestly).

As it currently stands, there's no release date for Boars in Rome, but there is a playtest you can sign up and gain immediate access to if you fancy a go yourself; you can do so on Steam right here, or at least pop it a wishlist.

#3968. Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection announced for PS5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, PS4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC

Atari publishing label Infogrames and developers Graphite Lab and Implicit Conversions have announced Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection, a collection of seven Lucky Luke games from Game Boy Color, Super Nintendo Entertainment System, PlayStation, and Game Boy Advance. It will launch for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC via Steam on January 13, 2027.

Here is an overview of the collection, via Infogrames.

Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection brings seven Lucky Luke titles from the 8-, 16-, and 32-bit eras to all modern platforms for the first time.

Lucky Luke: The Lonesome Cowboy Collection includes

Every game features quality-of-life improvements, including improved graphics, save states, achievements, visual filters, custom screen bezels, and rebindable controls. “How to Play” guides onboard unfamiliar players and help them solve difficult challenges.

The bonus Frontier Experience is an interactive first-person museum and shooting gallery that allows players to explore the history of the iconic gunslinger firsthand. Players can explore western locales, enjoy target-shooting minigames, search for collectibles and discover original comic and character art.

The legendary Lucky Luke originated in 1946 with a French-Belgian comic book about a street-smart gunslinger famous for shooting faster than his own shadow. Over the past 70 years the cowboy has gone on to feature in numerous comics, several animated television series, feature films, and most recently a 2026 live-action television series.

The Lonesome Cowboy Collection reunites Infogrames with the popular western franchise. Infogrames published several Lucky Luke titles in the late 90s and early 2000’s, including the incredibly rare Playstation Platinum edition of Lucky Luke: Western Fever.

The collection includes four games that were only released here in Europe and never made it to the United States, including the 1997 Super Nintendo Entertainment System release of Lucky Luke, the 2000 Game Boy Color release of Lucky Luke: Desperado Train, the 2001 PlayStation release of Lucky Luke: Western Fever, and the 2001 Game Boy Advance release of Lucky Luke: Wanted!

#3967. Mass Effect petition has enough signatures for the Canadian Government to potentially save BioWare

Following news of EA's decision to shut down iconic RPG studio BioWare, Canadian fans of the studio have escalated their grievances to the governmental level, calling on the Canadian Government to step in and save the Canadian studio from closure, seemingly after Canada's New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis called on the government to do so.

Fans have submitted a petition to the Canadian House of Commons arguing for the government to find a way for BioWare to continue, such as through funding that allows the studio to buy the Mass Effect and other IPs and go independent.

The petition, number e-7898, argues that "BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports" and that the studio's closure by its American parent company "represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," it continued.

The petition opened for signatures on 4th of November, and has already amassed 1,700 signatures. By law, petitions that surpass 500 valid signatures from Canadian citizens or residents are entered into the House of Commons' agenda, meaning they will be presented in front of the parliament.

As encouraging as that may be, it's worth keeping in mind that it may not result in meaningful change. Even if the Canadian Government agrees with the petition's goals, it cannot force EA to sell BioWare or its various IPs.

EA notably didn't shop the studio around before closing it down, and the publisher has a history of closing down owned studios rather than selling them off. EA has also kept the IPs of its various shuttered studios.

The community's reaction to BioWare's closure has taken different forms. Hundreds of thousands signed a different petition to save Mass Effect. The people behind the movement have purchased billboards in Times Square in New York City to advertise it, with plans for more outside The Game Awards ceremony in December.

Meanwhile, former BioWare developers have spoken about the last days of BioWare, and the work they've poured into Mass Effect Universe, the studio's final project before it was shuttered.

#3966. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for waking up covered in sand. The roof of your house is missing. A small man stands in the emptied bed of a dump truck. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he says. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he repeats. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," he declares once again, beginning to move towards you this time. "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6." You realise your hands are tied down. Oh no.

Is he about to sit on your face? WAIT, THAT'S NOW ILLEGAL HERE IN THE UK. NO, PLEASE, DON'T SIT ON MY-time seems to slow as the bare backside approaches your visage. As its cheeks prepare to become as sandy as yours, you hear its wielder say: "And we thought, hey, given the moment..."

Panicking, you scrabble for anything to say which might free you before something that might get a British MP's hackles up can occur. "Things first went awry when I turned up for my appointment to find a tall German man wearing a cowboy hat asking a PR if he could play the game," you blurt out. The posterior momentarily stops moving towards you. Buoyed, you continue to tell a story you heard from VGC's Chris Scullion.

I was asked if I minded sharing my one-to-one appointment with this chap too, to which my inherent British cowardly courtesy kicked in and I lied that it was perfectly fine.

"I want drums", he said as he entered the room. "We are playing Dani California by Red Hot Chili Peppers." Rather than ask him whether he also fancied telling me where I was going for dinner later, I picked up my guitar and went along with it, eager to just play the game.

The bottom begins its agonising crawl towards your kisser once more. You can feel the occupants of parliamentary benches begin to sense a disturbance in the force. Maybe if you can make the bumholder sad, that'll do the trick. You try to remember how Sebastian Cardoso of Game Studio Unlocked's presentation on the tragic fates of game studios after acquisitions went.

A hundred and twenty-three of the 362 developers were shut outright. The average life from acquisition to closure is 6.4 years and the median is 5, meaning half of all closed studios were dead within five years of their acquisition.

The familiar names mostly died fast. EA closed Pandemic two years after buying it. Sony shut Firewalk barely a year and a half in. Warner Bros. closed Player First roughly seven months after acquiring it. Bluepoint, closed at the five-year mark, is exactly what the median looks like.

It's no use. That arse's shadow its creeping across ever more of your face like your're a planet with a nose and it's the Vogon Constructor Fleet. Maybe you can somehow contort your head to the side. Arrrggghh. You call on all the strength of muscles you barely ever use and think of the incredible gymnastic feats executed by Physical Contortion Gamer's Josh Wolens during an ongoing GTA diary series.

Attempting to do flips, then, just sort of rotates your entire body below the diaphragm while your head and chest area remain bolt upright, rigid in such a way that you could feasibly fly a flag from your own thorax.

Which looks odd. Nevertheless, it is pretty fun to scoot and roll your way through Los Santos. At one point, I attempted a double frontflip in the middle of a part of the map that had been deleted for some reason. It didn't quite work out, and I ended up colliding with and possibly killing a man in a fursuit.

It doesn't work. You can't get away. You begin to scream. The posterioperator stops repeating the words "You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6". Instead, he asks where that mysterious German cowboy you mentioned earlier has gone. You don't have a clue, and can't help admitting as much. "Ah well." The derriere resumes its descent, now mere inches from your mug. This is the end. You have one last rummage through your mind for possible solutions.

Respec's Tom Orry hasn't managed to save you. "Fine, sit on my face and send me to hell," you shout into the pinkish ring of doom as British cops prepare to ram-raid your abode and arrest you for crimes against a prude's definition of acceptable shagging.

The bum stops. Its owner asks if you've just said the word Sentinel. "Yes," you lie.

The arse is raised and swapped for the face of a man. "What a perfect time for you to realise what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called," he says.

You notice he's not Todd Howard. Or Adrian Edmondson.

"It's Ade's month off and they needed another baldy to play this esteemed role," Sir Patrick Stewart announces, clearly responding the look of befuddlement your face can still have since it hasn't been crushed by a ten-tonne tush. You wonder how you didn't recognise his voice before, especially given he played the emperor in Oblivion.

"Here's to the next Bethesda game after Starfield," the Stew sings as the police bust through the door and he's beamed up before they can tackle him.

As the refounding theory finally starts to settle in, now we've got a shifting Great Calamity to deal with

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Legend of Zelda timeline has gotten yet another confusing new update, shifting the events leading to Breath of the Wild by 9,900 years and directly contradicting established lore. It's such an about-face for the existing story that series fans are pretty sure it's just a mistake, but the new word comes straight from Nintendo of America, which is often treated as gospel.

The Zelda timeline splits into three different branches based on the end of Ocarina of Time, but those branches all converge in the misty history leading up to the events of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. Earlier this year, Nintendo updated the Japanese version of the timeline and made clear that the founding of Hyrule depicted in flashback during Tears of the Kingdom shows the start of a new Hyrule, well after the one depicted in Ocarina of Time and other games has faded into history.

Now, Nintendo of America has updated the official English-language timeline to confirm the refounding – well, I say "confirm" but I'm sure it'll remain contentiously debated among the most dedicated purists. Either way, the update has made another curious tweak to the rest of the backstory.

Up until now, we've understood the timeline depicted in Tears of the Kingdom's flashbacks like this: Hyrule is (re)founded, Ganondorf appears to invade, and is sealed away as part of the Imprisoning War. Untold generations pass, and the evil entity known as Calamity Ganon eventually emerges and ravages the kingdom before being pushed back by Sheikah technology. 10,000 years pass from that Great Calamity, and that brings us to Breath of the Wild. Calamity Ganon reemerges, Link hibernates for 100 years, and the game begins.

According to the new timeline, the Imprisoning War happens, 9,900 years pass, and then the Great Calamity happens. Then it's just 100 years before Ganon reemerges – now referred to as "the second Great Calamity" – kicking off Link's century-long hibernation leading into Breath of the Wild.

In other words, the first Great Calamity, which was originally placed 10,000 years before Breath of the Wild, now takes place just a century or two before the game's events. This is despite the fact that Breath of the Wild is full of people trying to unlock the secrets of a pre-Calamity world that's long since faded into myth.

How are Zelda fans taking the sudden break in established lore? Well, you can read the Reddit threads for yourself, but I imagine you can already guess the tone of the responses. The Zelda timeline is notoriously convoluted, and while Nintendo has kept it up since at least 2003, Shigeru Miyamoto always maintained that it's "not that important to us."

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

Perhaps that's why Eiji Aonuma shut down attempts to add further nods to the timeline Ocarina of Time, and why a new official timeline update can so suddenly make an astronomical shift to established lore. Don't worry – regardless of how this detail shakes out, I'm sure the timeline will be broken in all-new ways soon enough.

Nintendo pulled back the horror from one of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake's most terrifying enemies: "Maybe we've gone a step too far."

#3964. World of Warcraft: Forever's seemingly stellar launch continues as it soars to the top of Twitch's most viewed games, beating out the likes of League of Legends and Zelda

World of Warcraft: Forever launched last night after a hugely successful beta, and it's not just players getting in on the fun. Blizzard's MMO is also proving quite the attraction for spectators, soaring all the way up to the top of Twitch's most viewed games.

As of writing, World of Warcraft sits at around 385,000 viewers and streamer Ahmpy has the most popular WoW channel, pulling in around 18,300 live viewers.

For comparison, Twitch's ever-popular non-gaming Just Chatting category is the service's second most watched category with 145,000 viewers, and Riot Games' genre-leading MOBA League of Legends takes third place with 81,400 viewers.

Aion 2, another MMO released back in October, is sitting pretty at around 75,900 viewers, while Nintendo's newly released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (it's good!) has brought in a wonderful 63,100 watchers on the day of its arrival.

Perhaps contributing to World of Warcraft: Forever's success is the fact it launched with few problems, enjoying one of the smoothest day-one releases in the series' recent history. Its beta proved especially popular, with Blizzard developers calling it one of the most successful betas they've ever seen. One wonders how many of these current Twitch viewers are adults getting their WoW fix during work while their boss isn't looking?

#3963. Ahead of The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past, here's a "lore friendly unofficial expansion to Geralt's life in Toussaint" from a well-established quest modder

While its remastered upgrade might have broken cover in late September, The Witcher 3's extra expansion isn't set to join it until next year. With 2027 still a month and a bit away, a modder's taken it upon themselves to add a few more adventures to Geralt's time in Toussaint, Blood and Wine's gorgeous French-ish duchy, before the bloke from the river heads off to Letten for Songs of the Past.

So far, only the opening chapter of the mod - Annals of the Duchy - has been released. It adds in a new quest about Geralt, with help from either Yen or Triss if either have made the trip out to Toussaint as part of your playthrough, getting into a scrape thanks to a halfling who seems to promise Gerry the chance to juice up his vineyard's vines.

The mod's creator, Jontej, has previously put together a couple of other custom Witcher 3 quests. While they do look to have used AI voices in English versions of those mods, for Annals of the Duchy they've enlisted a cast of human actors for both Enlish and Polish versions.

Jontej has plans to expand this new questline going forwards, having cited specific "plans for an extra storyline involving Syanna", whom you might remember from Blood and Wine's main quest. Given that - spoilers ahead - the mod relies on you having gotten the Blood and Wine ending which sees both Anna Henrietta and Syanna survive, as well as having paid to renovate the gardens of Geralt's vineyard. They add that, when it comes to their additions, the "timeline fits quite well [with] the upcoming official Songs of the Past Expansion, which has been confirmed to take place after the events of the main game/Blood and Wine".

As much as I've argued that, as of right now, I struggle to see how Songs of the Past will manage to outdo Blood and Wine as a satisfying end to Geralt's tale in the Witcher game trilogy, I am intrigued by the idea of a few more modded adventures showing Gerry adjusting to the semi-retired life. After all, Toussaint's got to have a few more dungeons tucked away that're worth temporarily dusting off the White Wolf's twin swords for.

To kick off Annals of the Duchy, you'll need to trigger its first quest by taking a stroll from the Corvo Bianco manor house down to its gardens between 11am and 1pm. It's worth noting that any other mod which messes with Yen, Triss or companions in general has a chance to muck things up as far as Jontej's creation goes.

"It's a guilt by association pattern that all developers need to push back on"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney has been in a bit of a one-sided beef with Valve co-founder and CEO Gabe Newell for a while now, lately about Steam's AI disclosure that requires developers to include a label informing Steam users of AI-generated content. Sweeney has had a number of complaints about Valve's storefront over the years, which makes sense as he owns one of its main competitors, the Epic Games Store, but he's been doubling and tripling down on the AI disclosure issue as of late. In a new interview, he not only sharply rebukes the AI label, but embraces AI in game development to degree rarely seen by him or other industry leaders.

Talking to GamesBeat, Sweeney gives one of the most bullish takes on AI generation in games I've seen in my many years covering this topic. Get on-board or die, is essentially his perspective.

"It's really clear to me that large-scale game developers–setting aside indies, where there's always going to be specialties and niches, large-scale game development will be totally changed by AI," Sweeney says. "Teams that don't adopt it will absolutely be left behind and rendered uneconomical, non-viable compared to their peers."

Sweeney says he's against any kind of legislation to curb the use of AI in game development in the US because it would give other countries the advantage. "Everyone is going to be adopting it," he says. "When one team can make a game four times more efficiently – 10 times more efficiently soon, perhaps – than another team can make the same game, there's just no possibility of competing the old way. No game developer has 75% to 95% profit margins that they can put at risk by not being as productive as possible."

There has been massive backlash to AI in games from players, voice actors, artists, and indie developers, but messaging from big studios and publishers generally ranges from cautiously optimistic to vocally and enthusiastically supportive. Meanwhile, a report from GDC found that 55% of respondents said AI was having a negative impact on the industry. Still, Sweeney wants to make sure companies aren't being bullied into choosing human workers over AI.

"Because there's a big resistance movement against AI that seems concentrated on trying to bully developers into not adopting it by attacking individuals, by review-bombing projects and so on, I've been trying to make my views known to as many game developers as possible," he says. "We have to power through this and build awesome games, use maximum acceleration, because it is a survival issue for all the companies in the industry."

Sweeney has called Valve's AI policy "abhorrent," politically motivated, and nonsensical among other things, and we can add another descriptor to the pile today: toxic. When GamesBeat pushes back and suggests Steam's AI label is there to inform players, Sweeney says he doesn't "buy it in the slightest," pointing to Steam's user review system as a means to let players know about "a game's quality, scope, entertainment value and so on." Ultimately, he says AI can be a force for good and bad in game development, and he sees Valve's mandatory disclosure as a judgment on the technology as a whole.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"You can build good games and bad games without AI. You can build good games and bad games with AI. You can repeat those distinctions for all engines, all development tools, all methodologies, all countries of origin, all teams and so on," says Sweeney. "If we were to identify AI as associated with bad games, that's just unfair to developers who use AI to make good games. It's a guilt by association pattern that all developers need to push back on."

Sweeney argues that Steam's AI disclosure is "being used toxically here, because it's absolutely being used by anti-AI advocates to undermine the reputations of developers and the viability of their projects."

Newell himself has yet to respond to Sweeney's many tirades, but prominent former Valve developer Chet Faliszek hit back in a YouTube video in which he called Sweeney's behavior "AI psychosis." Faliszek also argued that Sweeney was "treating all the players like children" and advised him to "act as a player yourself for a moment and go, 'What would I want to know about a game?'"

Why so many game developers don't want to use generative AI

#3961. Rockstar were "definitely" thinking about giving a Japanese studio the keys to GTA, says former tech director - "I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it"

Obbe Vermeij on ancient plans for a GTA Tokyo

Since time immemorial, North American and European publishers have racked their brains over ways to make their games sell in Japan, ancient heartland of mythical beings like Mario, Sonic, and Polaroid Pete. In the late noughties, Microsoft launched a big push to give Japanese youth the Xbox virus with such targeted console exclusives as Blue Dragon and Lost Odyssey. And Rockstar once dreamed of making a Grand Theft Auto game set in Tokyo.

Speaking to me last week, Rockstar North's former technical director Obbe Vermeij shared a little about the abandoned project. Emphasis on the "little" – it doesn't appear to have gotten very far, despite recently unearthed allusions to "Tokyo PS2" in GTA 5's source code.

Rockstar's parent company Take-Two Interactive filed a trademark for GTA Tokyo back in 2003, the year before the release of the Los Angeles-flavoured GTA: San Andreas. At the time, Rockstar were apparently looking at collaborating with a Japanese studio on the project. "So this was kind above my pay grade," Vermeij told me. "But yeah, there were negotiations with studios, and I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it, because then it becomes like a bigger thing than it is, and I'll probably get it wrong, and I don't know how far the negotiations were, how serious it was. I mean, it was definitely serious. It was the plan. But I don't know how close it got to actually happening."

The game itself would likely have been a contemporary story, not a historical yarn like Rockstar's subsequent Red Dead Redemption. "It definitely had samurai swords in it, I remember that, but I think it was present-day probably," Vermeij went on. "Or sort of not too [far off] - it wasn't, like, sort of the medieval era in Japanese history, or anything. It was definitely not like that."

Vermeij was at Rockstar from 1995 to 2009, where he worked on the first four mainline 3D GTA games, plus some handheld spin-offs. During that time, he says, Rockstar frequently considered the idea of a Grand Theft Auto set outside the United States. "In the same way that we were always thinking about other games, we also thought about cities that would be cool, and it was always the same list," he said. "It was Moscow, London. Istanbul, Rio de Janeiro, maybe Paris and Tokyo. It was always the same ones that people suggested."

Grand Theft Auto has never quite the money-spinner in Japan that it is in North America and Europe. Localised editions of the original three 3D GTA games were published by Capcom, sometime after the original releases, selling a few hundred thousand copies apiece in their launch years.

"I think perhaps [Rockstar's co-founders] the Housers were a little annoyed that GTA wasn't as big in Japan as they thought it deserved to be," Vermeij reflected. "So it kind of made sense to get a local studio to do it. Japanese people actually kind of like different games from westerners a fair bit. For instance, they don't like first person shooters and stuff. So, it made sense to have a Japanese studio have a shot at it, and I think it would have been really cool, because you know, a GTA made by somebody else in Japanese culture – that's something I would probably play."

Take-Two ultimately abandoned their original "GTA Tokyo" trademark in 2008. It's not clear how much Rockstar have considered setting GTA overseas since Vermeij's day, but co-founder Dan Houser (who left the company in 2020) recently told podcaster Lex Fridman that they ultimately decided it wasn't a credible objective.

“We made a little thing in London 26 years ago - GTA London - for the top-down for PS1," he said. "That was pretty cute and fun, as the first mission pack ever for PlayStation 1. I think for a full GTA game, we always decided there was so much Americana inherent in the IP, it would be really hard to make it work in London or anywhere else. You know, you needed guns, you needed these larger-than-life characters. It just felt like the game was so much about America, possibly from an outsider's perspective. But that was so much about what the thing was that it wouldn't really have worked in the same way elsewhere.”

If this article has left you pining for the Shibuya Scramble NPC-tipping sim that will never be, I bring good news: Japanese developers are quite capable of making their own urban open worlders. The obvious go-tos are Sega's Yakuza/Like A Dragon games, with their abundance of lovingly modelled eateries and discount stores. There's also Ghostwire: Tokyo, a respectable first-person parkour sim, though this particular incarnation of Tokyo has a lot of paranormal congestion. All these games have the advantage of being playable on PC right now. As for GTA 6? Who can say, but Vermeij thinks Rockstar might want to port it sooner to get ahead of the slopcomp craze.

#3960. Nintendo says it isn't planning any more Switch 2 price hikes

Nintendo, which unveiled the results of the first half of its fiscal year 2027 earlier today, has now said it has access to enough quantities of memory to manufacture more Switch 2 consoles.

As a result, the platform holder does not plan to increase the price of the Switch 2. That's according to Reuters, citing Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa.

Nintendo, which has so far sold 26m Switch 2 consoles, has already raised the price of the console earlier this year. The price hikes, which took effect on 1st September in the US, Canada, Japan and Europe, saw the console's price increase by $50 / €30 / ¥10,000. Although that was technically the first price hike for the console itself, prior to the Switch 2's launch last year, Nintendo raised the price of Switch 2 accessories in the US as a result of the Trump Administration's tariffs.

The reason that would cause Nintendo to raise prices again is the same that already caused rival PlayStation and Xbox to do so: AI-driven, global memory and storage shortages.

PlayStation already raised PS5 and PS5 Pro prices, on several occasions. Xbox has likewise gone through multiple rounds of price hikes for its Series X and Series S consoles, with the most recent having taken place in August.

That same crisis pushed one of Nintendo's longtime ROM suppliers to exit the business, opting instead to focus on the more lucrative business segments. ROM memory is used in Switch cartridges, though Nintendo hasn't commented on the news.

Incidentally, Switch 2 hardware sales have been in decline for several quarters now compared to its banner launch in 2025. Still, Switch 2 sales are tracking ahead of the Switch 1.

Welcome to the new era, folks, where we increasingly seem to be heading closer to a daily coin flip over whether our core online services stay live or go down. This time, it's Microsoft. Down Detector reports problems with Microsoft 365 services since about 12:30 pm (ET) yesterday, November 12, and issues are still ongoing.

Countries across the world are affected, and some institutions have been affected severely. Parts of the UK government, for instance, are having problems sending and receiving emails. The UK's health service, the NHS, has reportedly said it is unable to access online consultation for patients. The US and other governments have reportedly been impacted, too.

Microsoft explains that certain features of services "that interact with Exchange Online and email services are impacted." So, it looks like Exchange Online could be the culprit. This is the back-end of Microsoft services that use calendars, tasks, emails, and so on.

Affected services include MS365 admin center, apps, Education features, Copilot, Defender for Office 365, Defender XDR, Fabric, Graph, Intune, Planner, Power Apps, Purview, some elements of Teams, To Do, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

In other words, a very extensive list. It's also a list that a bunch of institutions and companies rely on to manage their day-to-day, thus why this is such a big deal.

The latest update from Microsoft, at the time of writing, explains:

"Recovery actions are ongoing and have progressed in phases across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure. Global telemetry and customer reports show incremental improvement in several workloads; however, service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"Network and traffic-management actions remain active. To protect email during recovery, we’re continuing to prioritize queue and backlog processing, and the email timeout window has been extended to 48 hours to preserve delayed messages.

"At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident. We will continue to treat this with urgency until full mitigation, and we will share a full Post-Incident Report with root cause and defense-in-depth actions after mitigation is complete."

That there is "no evidence of malicious activity" as the cause is promising, but it doesn't stop this from being a severe event that's causing a ton of problems in a ton of countries.

This is the big risk of relying on a single kind of service for all your important online dealings. We saw the same risk bear fruit last year with a global AWS outage that took out a load of online services for a while, and recently we saw similarly widespread issues as a result of PHP vulnerabilities.

We're seeing more and more as time goes on that services from big, usually-reliable companies aren't immune to catastrophe. Let's hope Microsoft figures this one out ASAP.

#3956. "There is no excuse for what I did," Nvidia CEO says, as affair with an alleged Chinese spy makes the US-China AI race look even more ridiculous

Just saying, Jensen, this probably doesn't happen if you stick to gaming GPUs

Ostensible graphics card company and definite AI giants Nvidia have commissioned an independent investigation into themselves, amid reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Per both the New York Times and Nvidia themselves, Nvidia offered to go under the microscope after US intelligence organisations elected to investigate Huang’s paramour, Chinese national Alice Huang (no, uh, relation, and also known as Huang Le), on suspicion of sharing sensitive information with Beijing. The Nvidia-running, leather-jacketed Huang has thus far only copped to an unspecified affair, admitting in an extraordinary public statement that he was "unfaithful to my wife." Still, the two investigations are likely to start a bizarre new leg in the alread-messy AI arms race that the US and China have been indulging in for years.

See, the basis for Huang and Huang’s relationship appears to be the same thing that’s been fucking us as PC owners: data centres and AI hardware. Alice Huang is a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company who’ve bought billions of US dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips – and have been investigated for allegedly getting some of them into the hands of Chinese companies, in defiance of US trade restrictions on goods that might threaten the States’ AI dominance. Possibly also, given both countries’ increasing interest in the technology’s military uses, their perception of national security.

Many of these embargo-dodging accusations originate from after Alice Huang left Megaspeed, though she is now under that separate investigation for intelligence-sharing, and the prospect of any high-tech pillow talk from the lips of someone like Jensen Huang would be very disturbing to the feds indeed. Both Nvidia and their "deeply sorry" CEO deny that he shared sensitive information beyond that required for routine customer/client discussions.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the company’s statement reads. "Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

In the US-Sino battle of artificial intelligence, Jensen Huang has – as with his marriage – played both sides. He’s undoubtedly been a, perhaps the driving force behind reinventing Nvidia from beloved makers of gaming gear to the US’ number-one purveyors of environment-ruining, brain-polluting slop technology. But after the Biden administration banned American-made GPU exports to China over fears they’d be used to boost the latter’s military capabilities, Huang successfully lobbied Donald Trump into relaxing those restrictions, allowing Nvidia to flog their wares – including their crème de la crème AI GPU, the H200 – to cash-rich Chinese companies.

In a further twist, many of those chips have got mysteriously stuck in Hong Kong import facilities, suggesting the Chinese government in fact wants AI companies to stick to Chinese-made parts. But then, the Hangzhou-based DeepSeek reportedly trained their latest AI model on illicitly-gained Nvidia tech, so there’s either a healthy black market in operation, or the CCP is willing to tolerate the occasional bit of decadent Western silicone if it helps them catch up to the burger-chomping likes of ChatGPT and Claude. Maybe both, and either way, one can see how a well-placed honeypot could prove useful. Allegedly.

Without wanting to pick sides, in a race where I hope both teams lose, it’s also China who have more work to do. The People’s Republic produces a greater proportion of successful 'open' AI models, where the inner workings and even source code is made public, and mines more of the crucial minerals needed to build components and infrastructure. However, US-produced 'closed' models dominate global AI usage, and despite the lack of minerals, its existing data centres are estimated to wield 40 times the combined compute power of China’s. Probably because they just get all the RAM they need from Best Buy instead of digging it up themselves.

#3955. Marvel Legendary 2nd Edition review: "Reboots an already-great card game into something even better"

The Marvel Legendary 2nd Edition Core Box improves on the original in nearly every way, delivering what remains one of the best classic deck building systems out there. For Marvel and deck builder fans that may have missed out on the original box, this is an incredibly easy recommendation, but for folks that may just want to replace their old box, you will need to weigh whether the elements here are worth it.

One of the best cooperative deck builders out there

Some great new art and the new neoprene playmat is a nice step up

Includes improvements that were originally added expansions are now included right from the start

Compatible with already released Marvel Legendary products

Did not really improve the storage solution or alleviate setup/teardown hassle

Not as strong value proposition for owners of the original core box

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

When it comes to the deck building genre of card games, these popular options have featured all manner of different properties and styles over the years, with one of my favorites being Legendary: A Marvel Deck Building Game (henceforth referred simply as Marvel Legendary) from Upper Deck. In fact, this was where I first got my introduction to the deck builder landscape; ever since watching Wil Wheaton's Tabletop episode featuring it, this has been one of my go-to types of games to play.

Now, Upper Deck has released a new edition of the base Marvel Legendary, bringing with it some refinements and updates that the team has picked up in the past 14 years since the original box came out, along with fan-favorite mechanics that were introduced in later expansion content. All of this results in superior, yet still very familiar, new starting point for anyone wanting to assemble some Marvel heroes and save the day – and one of the best card games overall for Marvel fans.

This new 2nd Edition of Marvel Legendary retains the same cooperative deck-building mission as the original, now with a nice neoprene mat gameboard, replacing the classic folding cardboard one. Prior to the game starting, players pick the heroes that they will build their decks with, a total of 15 choices, followed by the villain you will face off against, what their dastardly scheme will be, and the various henchmen and other foes assisting them.

From there, in typical deck-building fashion, over the course of numerous rounds, players will purchase and enhance their decks with hero cards from a shared pool, taking out villains, rescuing captured civilians, and thwarting enough of the mastermind’s schemes and bashing them in the face until either the heroes or villains come out victorious. It’s a tried-and-true formula that has served Upper Deck for many years and many spin-offs, and it all began with Marvel Legendary, and it still is just as fun today.

Players: 1-5Ages: 14+Game type: Deck-buildingComplexity: ModerateLasts: 30-60minsDesigner: Devin LowPublisher: Upper DeckPlay if you enjoy: Gwent, Magic: The Gathering

Legendary adopts a rotating and ever shifting marketplace of cards for folks to pick from, an approach more akin to Ascension as opposed to a static shop like Dominion. It’s an approach I have always favored, and considering all of the new redone art in this box, I appreciated this direction even more, since it lets me see more cards. Having each power of hero card feature its own unique piece of artwork is a great touch, that while fixed in later expansions, was sorely lacking in the original core box. Same with the various schemes you will contend with.

By and large, all the new artwork is an improvement, though some fall a bit flatter, with the “Wound” cards that will clog your deck. Previously, these featured a gruesome image of Wolverine getting blasted, his body contorting with pain as his classic X-men costume is shredded. Now, it’s just Iron Man in pristine looking armor holding his shoulder like he threw a slightly too-fast baseball, and pulled a muscle. I mean, I guess that’s a wound…technically?

For folks that don’t own the original Core Box of Marvel Legendary, this new box is an amazing and spectacular jumping on point for one of the most established deck builders out there. Even if you never touch any of the previously released expansions (that are compatible with this new box, by the way), you still have a fully stocked game that will keep things exciting for years to come. Things become slightly more complicated if you do already own the older box. At $100 msrp, it’s a hefty price tag for what is basically new artwork, some rebalanced cards, a couple and card types like sidekicks and S.H.I.E.L.D Officer Specialists being included (originally released in expansions).

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

Even when it comes to the heroes and villains being offered, there is a good deal of crossover between the two boxes. On the heroes side, Deadpool from the OG box has been swapped out for Miles Morales, and Doc Ock has been added to the Mastermind list to represent the web-head’s rogues gallery, along with some adjustments to the henchmen and villain offerings. Again, all of this is great for new players, it’s just something for returning owners to be aware of before they drop the cash on the new box.

There’s a reason that Marvel Legendary would go on to spawn tons of expansions, and with the Legendary series spinning off to feature other properties like The Matrix, Predator, and now even DC. It’s just a damn good game that has withstood the test of time.

Sure, it can still take a bit to set up and pack up, thanks to all the various little decks of cards you need to shuffle together, but the end result has always been worth the hassle. I look at my dinged up, faded, and scratched original core box sitting on my game shelf and remember back to all the fun game nights that it’s been a part of, and this new 2nd Edition Core Box will let the sweet prince finally rest. It’s served its time, and I can’t wait for the future game nights this new box will make.

✅ You like deck building games and don’t have the original core box: If you're a fan of the genre, you owe it to yourself to try this.✅ You're looking for a thematic cooperative game: Want something memorable to bring to your next game night? This is it.

❌ You already own the original box: You will need to weigh whether or not the new art and rebalanced cards are worth the price tag.❌ You prefer your deck building games to be purely competitive: Marvel is full of teams, so it's no surprise this spin-off follows the same formula.

#3954. Remakes and new games "both have a place in the stable" says Nintendo boss, buoyed by the success of Star Fox and Ocarina of Time

It's been a good year for Nintendo: between Star Fox - the N64 classic with a dazzling facelift on Switch 2 - and the newly-launched and utterly fantastic Ocarina of Time remake, the platform holder is having a good run. And that's before you get to the likes of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, Mario Tennis Fever or any of the Switch 2 re-releases of first-party Switch games, like Xenoblade Chronicles 3 or Animal Crossing: New Horizons.

As popular as its other games are, though, you have to admit that 2026 has been a banner year for Nintendo's remakes - both Star Fox and Ocarina of Time have commanded plenty of headline-grabbing attention over the past 12 months, and it's a fact that isn't lost on the company. In a new interview with Polygon, Nintendo's Nate Bihldorff - senior vice president of product development and publishing - says that wholly new games and remakes of classics are of "equal importance" to the publisher going forward.

"I do think that new games and remakes both have a place in the Nintendo stable, of equal importance to be honest," Bihldorff told the site at the Ocarina of Time's launch event in New York City. "There are fans of every single IP that we have out there. Of course, having new games in those series is wonderful, and I look forward to them as much as anyone else does, but there’s also a deep satisfaction in revisiting games that were very, very special, like Ocarina of Time… But it's also important to think about how many people had never played the original, and for them, the remake of Ocarina of Time is going to be an absolutely brand-new, 2026 experience, and one that I just cannot wait for them to get their hands on."

There's more interesting stuff in the interview, as Bihldorff outlines his views on the strenght of the Nintendo roster - "it doesn't matter how excited I am about Donkey Kong Bananza at launch; there's always going to be more games that are coming down the pipeline" - and that the release pipeline continues to look as strong for the Switch 2 as it did for the Switch. "There's one constant that has been consistent through my entire career at Nintendo, and that's that you can pretty much set your watch by the idea that we're going to be coming out with stuff," Bihldorff told Polygon.

Ocarina of Time is off to a very strong start; aside from being critically adored, the game has taken off virally - I can't move on my own feeds for clips of the game, people reminiscing about their original memories of certain locations, or long posts about the nostalgic elements of the title. Star Fox, meanwhile, has 1.17 million copies worldwide since its launch earlier this year on the Nintendo Switch 2, making it the ninth best-selling game on the platform (this is via Nintendo's financials yesterday). I expect Ocarina will outpace that.

Whatever your personal opinon on remakes in games, you cannot deny that it is a large part of the industry - and it seems Nintendo is keen to ride that wave as far as it'll go.

With all that said, when will I get my Pokemon Black and White remakes, then?

Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company after he admitted to an affair on Sunday, and allegations of a second affair came out on Wednesday. Now there are reports of a potential third. Though CTO Colette Kress has taken over in the interim, Nvidia seems to be shopping around for its next CEO, much to the dismay of some Nvidia staff, according to a report from Wired.

It's claimed that a longtime engineer at Nvidia took to an internal suggestion box this week to ask the Nvidia board to consider the company's employees before deciding whether or not to get rid of Huang. This note was made prior to his resignation.

However, over 1,600 comments have been left regarding this suggestion, the majority of which are apparently supportive of Huang. One says, "If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss."

Another claims, "We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance."

Notably, not all employees took to the suggestion box to air the same sentiment. One sent an email to the entire company saying, “I stand by Jensen. Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”

That email continues, “If America fails the man who helped build its future, then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

Jensen Huang's role in Nvidia can't be overstated. As the co-founder of the company, and President and CEO since 1993, he has no doubt been instrumental in its success. And business has been booming for the graphics card company-turned-AI company over the last few years.

No one knows how the Congress investigation will end up, but it's certainly not a great look for an active CEO to be questioned about this either way.

#3950. "The lesson learned is you can have both": Skyrim lead designer reckons there's merit in Baldur's Gate 3-style tough choices and Bethesda's do-anything approach

How many doors should be open at any point in an adventure?

Whether RPGs are better off prioritising player freedom or endeavouring to have several doors slam shut every time you put another foot forwards in order to encourage multiple runs with different characters is, to put it bluntly, something I reckon will still be a matter of debate in the year 4000. We'll all have evolved in non-corporeal beings floating in a galaxy that's been racked by such change that even the six million copies of The Elder Scrolls 5 we've littered the Earth with will have been swept away into the great recycling bin on the gods' desktop, and there'll still be sniping going on about whether it's ok that Skyrim lets you be a master thiefssassin who leads the companions, knows every spell under the sun, and slapped up a world-eating dragon for fun.

For what it's worth, the game's lead designer reckons both games that do and don't let you do that have their merits when executed well.

Speaking to The Examined Game, ex-Bethesda dev Bruce Nesmith talked about being "pleasantly surprised" when playing Baldur's Gate 3 just how much he enjoyed making "consequential decisions that closed off gameplay". In Nesmith's view, Larian "redefined things in a certain way" with their take on the D&D universe and the fantasy rules it plays by. However, he argued that there's still merit to taking an approach more akin to Bethesda's post-Morrowind Elder Scrolls entries and striving to make it possible for the player to see the majority of what the game has to offer in a single playthrough.

"They were both fun," he said. "They were just fun in different ways and that to me was part of the surprise. I would have expected to fall on one side or the other, as if they were things that you couldn't have both [of]. The lesson learned is you can have both. I can enjoy this game over here that does it this way and enjoy this game over here that does it that way."

Nesmith made clear that he still thinks the idea of, with a few exceptions like Skyrim's civil war, not gating the player off from the likes of doing multiple faction questlines is a "very good philosophy" that he supports.

As much as it's always a bit of a cop out to declare that everything's equally good, actually, I do think that there's merit in both approaches. I love the dedication the likes of New Vegas, Disco Elysium, and The Witcher 2 have to making you pick a path and see where it takes you at the expense of not seeing other stuff. Hell, the latter game's infamous for being totally different depending on who you choose to waltz off with at the end of the opening act.

That said, Skyrim's open-endedness was undoubtedly one of the factors which made it so easy for me to get majorly into when I was just cutting my teeth in RPGs as a teenager. There's value in such games existing, even if for plenty it might be as a gateway drug to games with crunchier and more challenging narratives that do demand you plug in your brain and carefully consider every choice you make. Whether there's still as much value in being the gateway drug nowadays compared to in 2011 is the question The Elder Scrolls 6'll likely answer whenever it rocks up. Coming as it is after the likes of BG3 and The Witcher 3 have had near Skyrim-level gangbusters success while leaning a lot more heavily into the hard stuff typically pegged as having less potential for mass appeal.

For what it's worth, while you can very much argue about the execution, Fallout 4's main quest was a lot more choice-heavy than Fallout 3's. So, Bethesda may well opt to pivot or make compromises in their player freedom-first ways if they feel some crunchier choice is in order.

#3949. After gobbling up EA, Saudi Arabia and private equity firm Silver Lake reportedly looking to buy Unity

After acquiring EA for $55bn earlier this year, Saudi Arabia and private equity firm Silver Lake are reportedly in the market for another massive video game company. And according to new reports, it's Unity.

Per Reuters, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) and Silver Lake - two major actors in the EA acquisition - are in talks to acquire the video game engine company for around $25bn. Silver Lake's Egon Durban already sits on the Unity Board of Directors, and the firm owns around eight percent of its shares already thanks to a $400m investment.

This $25bn valuation should be taken with a grain of salt for two core reasons. For one, it was decided prior to Unity's latest quarterly financial report, which included a 59% increase in strategic revenue year-over-year and net income of $122m. So this could propel the valuation upwards.

On the other hand, wider economic changes could have a detrimental effect. Reuters points out: "Strong ⁠growth in Unity's AI-powered Vector advertising platform helped it post its first quarterly profit on a GAAP basis since going public in September 2020." Given we've seen the generative AI sector take a major hit this week following the US midterm elections, it's possible companies using the tech may be viewed with more fiscal skepticism. Or, maybe this dip is just temporary. In short, take the $25bn valuation as a ballpark figure.

Unity has had something of an interesting past. There was of course the banana's runtime fee scandal of 2024 in which the company attempted to charge developers a fee on each game sale using the engine, which proved a PR nightmare and was quickly walked back. Unity also recently partnered with Google for AI-game creation platforms Google PlayGround and Unity Spark. Spark is shown to have created a Space Corridor game on its website that looks dubious at best - not exactly a resounding testament to the future.

The last time EA and Silver Lake bought something gaming related it was EA, a Western giant that would go on to lay off hundreds of staff and close BioWare months later. It is worth emphasising that the deal was a leveraged buyout, which saddles EA with substantial debt, whereas the exact nature of this proposed Unity deal is not confirmed. As such if it does happen, it may be a good ol' fashioned private acquisition, not this terms and conditions-laden deal that EA, in its newest guises, must contend with. We've already seen BioWare closed down as a result of this acquisition.

Expect more news about the Unity buyout when official information comes to light.

Now that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's latest remake is out in the wild, all eyes have turned to a certain smiling moon up above. But while fans speculate about the series' future, two former Nintendo marketing leads reckon a Majora's Mask remake is almost definitely on the way.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Switch 2 revival sold in droves earlier this month, moving more than 5 million copies in its first four days and leading to speculation about what comes next. For Kit Ellis and Krysta Yang (Nintendo of America's former marketing and PR leads), the series' future doesn't look so different to its past.

Speaking in the most recent episode of the Kit and Krysta podcast, the duo wonder if it's now a "foregone conclusion" that Nintendo will also remake Majora's Mask in the same style as Ocarina of Time's 2026 re-up. "I still think yes," Yang says. "They couldn't have been on the fence because they probably already started making it. I don't see why you wouldn't."

Nintendo pulled the same trick almost three decades ago when Majora's Mask came out less than two years after Ocarina of Time on the N64, which is almost unfathomable with how long 2026 development cycles can be. (Th two 3DS remakes also launched with little time in-between.) But Nintendo was able to pull it off because Majora's Mask smartly reused many of the assets, character models and systems that had already been built for Ocarina of Time - a feat it might be able to repeat once again.

"It may not be the next game," Ellis continues. "It may not be in the next one to two years, but so much of the foundational work has been done and it's the same work that let them make the original Majora's Mask very quickly after the original Ocarina on Nintendo 64… The ceiling has not yet been realized on Majora's Mask."

The duo also speculate that if Nintendo wants to release a Zelda game every year, it'll likely rotate between new 2D entries, new 3D ones, and remakes. A Majora's Mask remake built off of the Switch 2's Ocarina of Time seems like an easy decision.

"It just doesn't make sense for them not to do it," Yang adds.

#3947. PS5 QSSR support added to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, CONTROL Resonant, ARC Raiders, THE FINALS, No Man’s Sky, and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam

PlayStation 5‘s Quick Spectral Super Resolution—the base console equivalent of PlayStation 5 Pro’s artificial intelligence upscaling solution PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution—will add Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, CONTROL Resonant, ARC Raiders, THE FINALS, No Man’s Sky, and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam to its lineup of supported titles, Sony Interactive Entertainment announced.

“Having seen great results integrating [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] in Marvel’s Wolverine, our team decided to bring it to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 as well, in an update that’s live now!,” said Insomniac Games head of technology Mike Fitzgerald. “We’re excited for players to swing back into our 2023 title and see [Quick Spectral Super Resolution]’s exciting image stability and sharpness benefits in both Fidelity and Performance modes.”

Remedy Entertainment is bringing Quick Spectral Super Resolution to CONTROL Resonant on PlayStation 5, with noticeable improvements in image stability and fine detail.

“It’s great to see PlayStation bringing the same kind of leap on the PlayStation 5 that [PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution] brought to PlayStation 5 Pro,” said Remedy Entertainment senior graphics programmer Erik Jansson. “[Quick Spectral Super Resolution] gives CONTROL Resonant a much more stable and detailed image, and we’ve worked closely with Sony to have it ready in an update coming in December.”

“With the new [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] coming soon to ARC Raiders and THE FINALS, we can deliver increased sharpness, better environmental clarity and overall visual improvements to even more PlayStation players,” said Embark Studios technical art director Mikael Linderholm. “We are very happy to see Sony’s continued investment in PlayStation technology translate into meaningful improvements for all players, bringing more immersive experiences across the PlayStation ecosystem.”

“No Man’s Sky gives players an infinite procedural universe to explore,” said Hello Games founder Sean Murray. “When every star in the night sky is a real solar system players can visit, we care a great deal about the quality of every pixel.

“The team has always been passionate about pushing the boundaries of technology on PlayStation. [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] allows us to render the universe in sharper, cleaner and more beautiful detail, while delivering the best possible framerate. Look for it in the next few weeks.

“It’s another step towards making the universe of No Man’s Sky even more immersive to explore.”

“We’re delighted to confirm that we are adding [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] to Hell Let Loose: Vietnam on PlayStation 5 through an upcoming update,” said Expression Games game director Paul Rustchynsky. “Console visuals are something our community has been passionate about, and [Quick Spectral Super Resolution] will bring sharper, cleaner image quality to the battlefield, from dense jungle to the chaos of a full-scale firefight. We can’t wait for our PlayStation players to see the difference.”

#3946. Microsoft workers accuse company of trying to get customers "addicted" to AI while forcing it on their own staff and making them party to "human rights violations"

Open letter warns of "a cascade of business and ethics risks"

A group of "concerned Microsoft workers" have published an open letter criticising their employer's "speed-at-all-costs" approach to generative AI, which they argue is "harming our customers, colleagues, shareholders, vendors, and the planet". They accuse Microsoft leadership of trying to get people "addicted" to genAI, while making their own staff miserable by mandating AI usage.

Echoing the on-going BDS campaign against Microsoft's Xbox business, the writers contend that Microsoft have become party to "human rights violations" by selling generative AI technology to Israel's military during the latter's invasion of Gaza, which a UN commission has deemed a genocide. They're also critical of Microsoft's contracts with the USA's draconian Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. While seemingly not against generative AI in principle, they're organising against "the AI industry’s trajectory to continue to enrich AI’s powerful few", pointing out that AI companies now account for a terrifying share of the global stock market.

I know about the letter thanks to Vertical Slice, who cite a New York Times report on Microsoft's recent voluntary buyouts, which follow several waves of mass layoffs at a company with a market value of around $4 trillion.

"For many, working at Microsoft has become joyless and demoralizing, with job satisfaction declining around the same time the company accelerated its AI investments," the workers write. "Crushing workloads, threats of AI job replacement and layoffs, constantly shifting business priorities, and re-orgs destabilize our work environment and erode employee trust in leadership."

The letter organisers complain that "workers are forced to use AI in almost every work area, with little to no training and no strategic rationale besides 'speed'," obliging them to spend a lot of time "learning and relearning tools, fixing AI slop, and reworking or rolling back low-quality features". They feel that Microsoft's generative AI strategy is exposing customers "to overreliance, misuse, and physical and mental harm", not least because "our own research shows that AI agents don’t prioritize user safety, and internal planning documents detail how to 'make people addicted' to AI products." If that last part is an actual quote from an internal feature document, then: yeeeeeeesh.

The writers further take issue with Microsoft's investments in data centers for generative AI use, which may use up a lot of water while contributing to carbon emissions (jeopardising Microsoft's older commitments to reducing their carbon footprint). They note that "our Community-First AI Infrastructure plan makes vague financial and job-creation commitments, but doesn’t address greenhouse gas emissions or other damage already being done."

The organisers also call out their employer for becoming "a partner to human rights violations" by licensing generative AI tools to the Israeli military and ICE. "Not only are we risking reputational, financial, and legal damage, we are allowing our AI products to be used against whole communities for mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, and genocide," they write.

Finally, they take a swing at "Microsoft’s participation in circular investment across a handful of AI leaders " - that is, AI companies pouring cash into each other, which naturally creates the risk of several companies biting the dust if one company's fortunes take a tumble. This ouroboros strategy "exposes workers, customers, shareholders, and society to a cascade of business and ethics risks," the writers claim, noting that AI-linked stocks now dominate the S&P 500 index.

The letter writers have a number of demands. They'd like more say over "AI product strategy decisions", and for Microsoft to consider customer feedback and bring different development disciplines together "to help guard against shipping AI-worsened user experiences". They want Microsoft to "offer quality training and empower workers to integrate AI in their workflows without tying AI use to rewards, reprimand or layoffs." They call on the execs to "end unfair AI-driven workforce reductions and agree to worker protections".

Looking beyond Microsoft's walls, the workers argue that "job opportunities from data center investments are mostly temporary" and that "Microsoft must protect all workers, not attempt to avoid the unionized trades in local communities, and ensure a just transition for all impacted workers."

The letter writers call on Microsoft to "expand Responsible AI and Sensitive Use teams and fund programs to communicate potential harms to users". They would like Microsoft to stop selling AI materials to organisations "if they are engaged in violence, mass surveillance, detainment, deportation, or genocide", requesting that Microsoft "transparently share contracts with all governments and their agencies or contractors, including police and armed forces, and immediately terminate any contracts with those directly or indirectly involved in human rights violations."

The letter writers want Microsoft to "reduce financial dependency on OpenAI and other AI partners and provide transparency into all AI investments". In general, they want their bosses to "stop offloading financial risk to workers, vendors, partners, customers, and shareholders through irresponsible investments and relationships." As regards the environment, the workers are demanding that Microsoft "reaffirm our goal to be carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste by 2030". They want Microsoft to cooperate more with environmental regulators, and "to respect local communities by rejecting dirty energy, engaging fairly and transparently, and refusing to build in resource-scarce areas."

It's not clear who, exactly, is behind the letter, or how many others at Microsoft have signed as of writing. I've requested comment from Microsoft, and will update this piece as and when I hear more.

#3945. "Is there any accountability left in this world?" Warren Spector pops off at EA executives and their massive payouts as BioWare shuts down

It's only been two weeks since we last heard Warren Spector sound off about EA's sudden decision to close BioWare, following the publisher's acquisition by Saudi Arabia's PIF and venture capitalist concerns. But now, the storied developer is back and - apparently - angrier than ever.

"I recently posted my thoughts about EA’s shuttering of BioWare," Spector wrote in a post on LinkedIn. "Those of you who read my post know that I was unhappy. I remain so. The tragedy of so many layoffs the last few years hasn’t been lost on me, but for some reason, BioWare hit me on an emotional level that nothing before had. I felt gut-punched."

Spector goes on to counter the idea that the studio was closed down as a "sound business decision" because the "studio’s glory days (artistic and commercial) were behind them" and that "businesses don’t succeed on history alone". These reactions, more than anything else, appear to be what's inspired Spector to take to posting again - he simply cannot agree with this assessment.

"If studio-level people leave, resulting in dilution of talent, someone is creating an environment that pushes them out. Do those culture-killers pay any price? If executives misread the market, over-hire, or make decisions that result in under-funded, over-funded, poorly-marketed games do they lose sleep let alone jobs?" he asks.

"Do those same executives suffer like developers when the needs of financial partners and private investors take precedence over the people who actually create value, let alone over the interests of players? Does anyone up there in or adjacent to the C-suite care? Is there any accountability left in this world? Obviously not."

He then goes on to list the yearly payouts that some of the highest-level executives at EA are rewarded per annum. These include:

"Tens of thousands of do-ers and makers are out of work and these people think they're worth that kind of compensation?" continues Spector. "And if you think this is a discussion about 'sound business decisions', I hope you never get anywhere near running a business. Or at least that people have the sense not to go work for you."

Back in August, we saw Warren Spector announce his intention to retire from the world of video game development. Spector's announcement comes shortly after the last game he worked on - Thick as Thieves - had its final major update only a few months after its release. Despite its charm and low price, Thick as Thieves sadly didn't sell what it needed to, resulting in layoffs at Spector's studio.
